name: microservices-sprawl
context: ANTI-PATTERN. A system is decomposed into far more services than its complexity warrants — service counts ranging from a team of 60 with 20 services to a team of 4 with 200 — because the 'micro' was taken literally, because decomposition was driven by a normalised database view rather than by a domain boundary, or because every new hire triggered an extraction. Defining more services moves complexity from inside services to between them: each additional service makes development, testing and deployment harder, and diminishing returns set in once services are already small and fast to test. The result is a distributed monolith that lost the one thing distribution was supposed to buy.
benefits: Naming the failure mode precisely separates it from the microservices pattern itself, which is legitimate under real complexity
The diagnostic signals are concrete: a team of four owning two hundred services, CRUD-shaped services with no behaviour, coordinated releases, and a debug story that spans every service
The remedy is measurable — one service per team is the floor, and further splits should follow team growth, not table counts
Starting larger around a bounded context is explicitly the advised counter-move, so the anti-pattern has a constructive exit
tradeoffs: Documenting an anti-pattern does not prevent it — the incentives that produce it (independence per unit, per-team ownership) are the same ones the pattern sells
Pulling services back together is expensive and often politically impossible once contracts and deployments are coordinated across them
Severity is invisible until independent deployment fails, which is usually discovered during an incident rather than in review
The style is not wrong in the large-system limit, so the pattern must be argued from complexity, not from dogma
use_cases: Recognising an existing estate that needs consolidation back into a modular monolith or a smaller service set
Architecture review of a proposed decomposition before pipelines and per-service teams exist
Evaluating whether a candidate service boundary is a business capability or a database table
Planning a rollback or an inverted-extraction when services must be merged to restore independent deployment
Setting an explicit budget for service count against organisational capacity
avoid_when: The team is large, the domain genuinely bounded, and each service is owned and released by a durable team
Services are shaped around business capabilities rather than around CRUD resources
Deployments are demonstrably independent — a suite of services whose releases must be coordinated is not microservices
The operational platform (CI/CD, observability, on-call, service discovery) already exists and is exercised
component_types: Excess services: an order or magnitude more deployables than the team structure supports
Anemic CRUD services: one per entity or table, carrying no behaviour and all the coordination cost
Coordinated release train: services that must be deployed in lockstep, which negates independent deployment
Distributed monolith: technically separate, logically intertwined through synchronous calls and shared data
Coupling fabric: chatty inter-service calls whose failure and latency paths multiply with service count
Operational tax: the per-service pipeline, monitoring, alerting and on-call burden
technology_stack: Service mesh (retries and timeouts amplifying with call count)
anti_patterns: One service per database table or CRUD resource — the normalised view of the data is not a domain boundary
Splitting on team-size arithmetic before the teams exist, producing services nobody owns end to end
Coordinated multi-service releases, which means the deployment independence the architecture was bought for does not exist
Chatty synchronous call chains where half a dozen services call another half a dozen, and latencies compound
Creating services in a greenfield project rather than by splitting one that demonstrably outgrew a monolith
design_principles: Complexity of the system must justify the complexity distribution introduces
A service must be a business capability, not a table
One service per team is the floor, not the target
If releases need coordinating, it is not a microservice architecture
Complexity is moved into the interconnections, not removed
best_practices: Do not start a greenfield project with microservices; split a monolith that has actually outgrown itself
Size services by what the delivery and operations teams can independently release, monitor and operate
Before adding a service, ask what problem it clearly solves for maintainability or testability
Merge services that always deploy together until independent deployment is real, not aspirational
Keep module boundaries inside a modular monolith strong enough that the split stays unnecessary
references: Martin Fowler, Microservice Trade-Offs — complexity shifted to the interconnections between services, https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservice-trade-offs.html
Chris Richardson, Microservices adoption anti-pattern: More the merrier, https://microservices.io/post/antipatterns/2019/05/21/antipattern-more-the-merrier.html
Zhamak Dehghani, How to break a Monolith into Microservices — cambrian explosion of anemic services for CRUD resources, https://martinfowler.com/articles/break-monolith-into-microservices.html
Martin Fowler, Microservices Guide — Monolith First and baseline operational competencies, https://martinfowler.com/microservices/
